A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same forecasting framework, renamed from VIFO to VFEM, with matching architecture and retained results. All text, equations, tables and figures are readable. V1 has no appendix; v2's Appendix A is fully available.

before.justification: V1 reports original forecasting results on seven datasets and module ablations on ETTh1 and ETTh2 in Tables 2–3.

after.justification: V2 retains original forecasting results and adds fusion, freezing, representation-quality and spectral-input experiments, including Appendix A.

M1.justification: The default frozen vision encoder, temporal branch, projections, feature fusion and forecasting pipeline are retained under the VFEM name. V2 explains grayscale construction, embedding replication and attention operations more explicitly. Fusion, unfreezing and spectral alternatives are experimental comparison variants, not adopted revisions of the default method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate multivariate forecasting on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Electricity/ECL, Weather and Traffic. The new diagnostic and spectral-input studies reuse existing datasets without introducing another domain or forecasting scenario.

E2.justification: The main forecasting baseline roster is retained, but v2 Tables 2–3 include Chronos-Base/Large and Moirai-Base/Large on Traffic, where v1 Table 2 had no results. V2 also compares additional component-level alternatives in its ablations. Newly discussed VisionTS is not an evaluated forecasting baseline.

E3.justification: V2 adds controlled fusion and freezing comparisons, spectral-input substitution protocols, and representation evaluation using 500 training and 500 test sequences, K-Means with k=10, t-SNE and Silhouette Scores. Existing forecasting lengths and metrics remain unchanged. The zero-shot versus supervised distinction and optimizer settings are newly disclosed, not established changes to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: The original module-removal ablation is retained as Table 4. V2 adds six fusion alternatives, partial/full encoder fine-tuning comparisons, statistical/raw/projected embedding analysis, and five spectral-input alternatives in Appendix A. These substantially broaden tests of the framework's design choices and representations.

E5.justification: The reported repetition count increases from three runs in v1 Section 3.1 to five in v2 Section 4.1. Tables 2–3 first report VFEM means with standard deviations throughout the main benchmark comparison. Baselines and ablation tables still provide point estimates without comparable uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: All shared benchmark means and original module-ablation values are unchanged. V2 adds Traffic baseline results and substantial new analytical results: projected embeddings have test Silhouette Score 0.468 versus 0.135 for raw SigLIP2, and the tested spectral inputs do not improve forecasting over raw images. For example, ETTh1 at horizon 720 has STFT MSE 0.442 versus the default 0.401.

T1.justification: Neither version contains theoretical guarantees, formal assumptions or proofs. V2's equations detail the existing normalization, attention, projection, fusion and prediction operations; Appendix A describes standard transforms and tensor shapes. These expand technical specification without adding a theoretical argument or substantive mathematical result.

C1.justification: The central claims about visual cross-variable modeling, arbitrary variable dimensions, 7.45% trainable parameters and competitive forecasting remain. V2's conclusion additionally claims that freezing avoids overfitting on limited time-series data. Most other contribution changes consolidate wording or introduce supporting evidence for retained claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting freezing to preservation of pretrained representations, projection to domain adaptation and generalization, and spectral-input underperformance to mismatch with natural-image pretraining. Sections 4.2.3–4.2.4 and Appendix A also discuss modality-gradient differences and possible spectral-domain pretraining or alignment. These explanations were absent from v1.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands reproducibility information: grayscale channel replication, global-embedding expansion, normalization and attention details, dimensions and layer counts, Adam learning rate 10^-4, and 300 epochs with early stopping. It also identifies baseline-result provenance and supplies spectral-transform parameters in Appendix A. These are principally new disclosures, not demonstrated changes to existing settings.

R1.justification: A new three-part Related Work section substantially develops positioning against foundation models, cross-modal approaches and multivariate dependency methods. V2 explicitly distinguishes VFEM from VisionTS and adds references including Sundial, Time-MoE and Mamba-based work. The decoder-only foundation-model reference by Das et al. is removed.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction and method exposition, renames VIFO to VFEM, consolidates the contribution list, and reorganizes temporal and visual processing. Dedicated related-work, prediction/denormalization and analytical subsections substantially change the narrative structure beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout. The combined forecasting table becomes separate MSE and MAE tables with supervision-category headers and uncertainty displays. Existing figures are relocated, and new input-construction, embedding and spectral figures accompany three additional experimental tables.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's sparse implementation description and limited evidence for key design choices. Detailed specifications, baseline-provenance and supervision disclosures, uncertainty estimates, and targeted fusion/freezing/spectral experiments improve reproducibility and evidential support despite unchanged benchmark means. Some new claims about avoiding overfitting and strong generalization exceed what the freezing comparisons and clustering scores directly establish, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.
